summary: For ages 9–11, this procedural/evaluation topic has learners design weather-protective solutions (raised houses, flood barriers, aerodynamic roofs/tie-downs, tornado shelters, early-warning systems), explain how each feature counters a hazard mechanism, and — the distinctive 9–11 grain — EVALUATE advantages AND limitations, pushing each design past its limit so failure is discovered rather than asserted. A design-test-evaluate cycle is the core activity; a defend-your-choice panel discussion and knowledge checks are valuable complements.
misconceptions: A good design makes a building weather-PROOF — solutions reduce impact but can be overwhelmed; hazards can't be eliminated
The strongest/most expensive solution is always best — merit depends on cost, feasibility and the specific hazard
One solution fits every hazard — flood, wind and tornado defences work differently
Early-warning systems physically stop damage — they reduce harm to PEOPLE by enabling action, not by protecting structures
If a design survived one event it will survive any event — performance depends on the event's magnitude

activities.title: Build-and-break weather-defence test bench
steps: Protect a coastal town within a fixed budget by choosing defences: raise houses, add a sea barrier, bolt on an aerodynamic roof, site a tornado shelter, wire up an early-warning siren.
Run the extreme event (flood, high wind, tornado) and watch which features hold.

Turn a design-LIMIT dial that raises the hazard magnitude until a solution is overwhelmed — e.g. a barrier that shrugs off a 2 m surge is overtopped at 3 m; a roof that survives a gale peels off in a hurricane (illustrative figures within the model, not measured thresholds).
Fill an advantages/limitations grid tallying protection level, cost, feasibility and the point where each design fails.
Note that the warning siren saves PEOPLE by enabling action even when it protects no walls.
activities.insight: No design is weather-PROOF: every solution reduces impact up to a limit and then fails, so 'best' means weighing how much protection you buy against cost and feasibility — and early warning reduces harm to people rather than to structures.

activities.title: Defend your design to a sceptical engineering/community panel
steps: Present a chosen solution, citing the test-bench data on how much protection it provides and at what cost.
Respond to probing questions in role: 'What happens in a bigger storm?' 'Is it worth the cost?' 'Would it protect against a different hazard?'
Justify a merit claim by weighing advantages against limitations, naming at least one genuine failure point.
activities.insight: Evaluating a design means defending its merit with evidence and conceding its limits, not asserting that one option is simply 'better'.

activities.title: Trace the mechanism: feature to hazard
steps: For each protective feature, trace a causal chain from the hazard to the house: a raised floor keeps floodwater below the living space as long as the water stays lower than the floor; roof straps tie the roof to the walls so it resists wind uplift up to the strength of the straps and fixings; a sea barrier holds back floodwater up to its height, provided it does not fail first.
Match each solution to the specific hazard mechanism it counters (uplift, floodwater depth, flying debris) and flag mismatches.
Explain why a flood barrier does not help against wind, and vice versa.
activities.insight: A feature works by countering a specific damage mechanism; whether a design helps depends on matching that mechanism and having enough capacity for the hazard's size (for example, barrier height compared with surge height), not on looks or on being big for its own sake.

checkQuestion: Show the child two engineering solutions for the same weather hazard (e.g. a raised/stilted house and a flood barrier for flooding; or a hurricane-strapped roof and a tornado shelter). Ask them to explain how each design feature reduces damage, then evaluate which is better and name a limitation of their choice — watch how they reason from the hazard to the feature. Set the task and observe; don't ask them to define 'engineering.'
checkAnswer: Explains the mechanism of at least one feature (a raised floor keeps floodwater below the living space; roof straps tie the roof to the walls so wind can't lift it), evaluates by weighing how well each reduces harm against cost and practicality, and names a genuine limitation (a barrier can be overtopped; a raised house is dearer and useless against wind).
